blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Choosing the right graph for the data, and completing a printed graph to the conventions of the page.

blocks.heading: The graph and its data
blocks.text: Each graph type suits its data. A line graph for values over time; a bar chart for categories; a histogram for grouped continuous counts; a divided bar or pie graph for shares of a total; a flow diagram for movement between places; a wind-rose for the frequency of winds from each direction; an isoline map for values spread over space; a scatter graph with a best-fit line for the relationship between two measures; a triangular graph for three shares totalling 100 per cent; a radial graph for cycles through the day; a dispersion graph for the spread of a value at many sites; a choropleth map for values by area; a kite diagram for proportions changing along a transect; a pictogram for simple totals. The data decides the graph, and the graph that distorts the data is wrong however neatly drawn.

blocks.heading: Completing a printed graph
blocks.text: Half-drawn graphs test convention as much as plotting. The completed part matches the printed part: the same scale, so the new bars rise against the same axis divisions; the key's shading, so a striped segment is striped, not solid; the key's order, so the pie's segments run clockwise from the top in the order the key lists; and bars from the correct end of the axis, so a horizontal bar chart grows from its baseline. A completed graph that ignores the printed half looks finished and reads wrong, and the test is whether it matches the others on the page.

blocks.heading: A completion worked through
blocks.text: Suppose a divided bar of a town's employment is printed with the primary and secondary segments shaded and the tertiary segment missing. The completion works in three checks. The scale: the printed segments sit on a 100 per cent bar, so the missing segment's width is the tertiary share of that whole, read off the axis. The order: the key lists primary, secondary, tertiary, and the printed segments run left to right in that order, so the missing segment joins the right-hand end, after secondary, not wherever space remains. The shading: the key's tertiary pattern is used, not a fresh one, because a completed graph that invents its own key cannot be read against the page. Three checks, and the bar is finished to the page's own conventions.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: These are the same techniques the data skills of topic 4 use, and every enquiry task in this topic ends with a graph to complete on the learner's own paper.
